standard.title: Changing Perspectives on Migration Since 1945
standard.description: the causes of changes in perspectives, responses, beliefs and values on migration that have influenced Australian society since 1945
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied changing perspectives and government policies in interwar Australia, including immigration and the White Australia Policy in its earlier form.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse how and why perspectives, beliefs and values on migration changed across Australia from 1945 to the present, examining the causes of those changes and their influence on Australian society and identity.

nodes.label: Changing attitudes across decades
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how community and government attitudes to migration changed across the 1950s to the 1980s, using sources to identify the causes of each shift.
nodes.minimum_width: Analyse how attitudes to migration changed across at least two decades since 1945, identifying at least one cause of each change.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse changing attitudes across the 1950s, 1960s, 1970s and 1980s using sources — from the guarded acceptance of European migrants in the 1950s, through the dismantling of the White Australia Policy (1966–1973), to the debates over Asian migration in the 1970s–80s and the emergence of multiculturalism; use sources to trace how public opinion, media representation, and government policy shifted in response to each other.
wider: Examine the Child Migration scheme (1922–1967) and the 2009 formal apology as a case study in how Australia's values and responsibilities toward child migrants were contested and later reassessed

Investigate the arguments for and against the White Australia Policy between 1964 and 1973 in detail, examining the sources — political speeches, newspaper editorials, migrant accounts — that reveal the range of views in this pivotal period
nodes.hinge_reason: The pattern of attitude change established here — government policy driving change, or community attitudes preceding policy — is the analytical framework needed for K13 (continuing efforts to create change) and for understanding why civil rights campaigns for migrants required sustained effort rather than single legislative events.

response_modes.reason: Students often describe attitude change as inevitable or progressive. Explicitly examine the causes and contingencies of change — asking 'what drove this shift?' at each transition point — to build a genuine causal analysis rather than a narrative of linear progress.

success_criteria: Describe how attitudes to migration in Australia changed across at least two different decades since 1945
Identify at least one cause of each attitudinal shift identified
Use at least one historical source to support a claim about changing community attitudes to migration

nodes.label: Multiculturalism and identity debates
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss the contribution of migration to Australia's changing national identity and analyse the debates over multiculturalism and contemporary immigration policy.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe how successive migration waves contributed to Australia's changing cultural identity and explain at least one debate over multiculturalism or immigration policy.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss how different waves of migrants — European 1950s–60s, Asian 1970s–2000s, Middle Eastern 1980s–90s, Indian 1990s–2000s, African 2000s — contributed to Australia's changing identity as a nation through cultural and religious diversity; discuss the debate over multiculturalism that emerged in the 1980s; analyse how immigration and border protection debates evolved from the early 1990s to the present — mandatory detention, humanitarian migration, business and skilled migration, temporary protection visas — examining how international events changed the terms of debate.
wider: Examine the Tampa affair (2001) and 'children overboard' incident as a case study in how security and compassion narratives compete in immigration debates — analysing the sources available and what they reveal about how the government managed public opinion
Compare Australia's multiculturalism policy with that of Canada or the UK, evaluating how similar policy frameworks produced different public debates and social outcomes

response_modes.reason: The contemporary immigration debates (mandatory detention, TPVs) are often treated as too political for classroom analysis. They are, however, the direct continuation of the attitudinal patterns traced in Node 1 — including them as legitimate historical material (with evidence-based analysis) honours the descriptor's scope.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The evolution of immigration debate from the White Australia Policy to mandatory detention is a rich longitudinal case study in how national values are negotiated over time — directly relevant to K13, K18, and K19, and to the S05 and S07 skills.
success_criteria: Describe how at least two different migration waves contributed to Australia's changing cultural identity
Explain the core debate over multiculturalism in the 1980s, identifying at least two competing positions
Describe how at least one aspect of Australian immigration policy changed between the 1990s and the present and explain what drove that change
